triage.reason: Secondary hypertension case with clues on history (resistant hypertension, bruit, flash pulmonary edema) and imaging workup; good differential with essential hypertension.

demographics: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is more common in older adults with widespread atherosclerosis
Fibromuscular dysplasia is much more common in women and typically presents at ages 15–50
More common in people with chronic kidney disease or refractory hypertension

risk_factors.text: Atherosclerotic disease elsewhere (coronary, carotid, peripheral, aortic)

family_history: Fibromuscular dysplasia in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: My blood pressure pills don't seem to be working anymore
My blood pressure has been really high even with three medicines
I get short of breath and my legs swell up
I feel tired and my legs are weak

hpi.onset: Gradual; hypertension may have been present for years and become harder to control, or may appear suddenly in a younger person
hpi.duration: Weeks to years; often discovered when blood pressure remains high despite multiple medications
hpi.progression: Blood pressure becomes progressively harder to control, requiring more medications; kidney function may decline over time, especially after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
hpi.location: Generalized; no specific pain location. Some patients note flank discomfort.
hpi.quality: Typically asymptomatic; symptoms come from uncontrolled hypertension or heart failure
hpi.severity: Variable; blood pressure often severely elevated (e.g., systolic >160–180 mmHg) despite treatment
aggravating: Starting or increasing an ACE inhibitor or ARB (can worsen kidney function)

associated_symptoms.text: Shortness of breath, especially when lying flat or at night
Sudden severe shortness of breath with pink frothy sputum (flash pulmonary edema)

pertinent_negatives: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
Recent sore throat or skin infection

positives.text: High blood pressure readings at home
Shortness of breath when lying flat
Waking up at night short of breath

atypical.how_it_differs: Renal artery stenosis is rare in children; when present it is usually due to fibromuscular dysplasia or a genetic syndrome and presents with severe hypertension, failure to thrive, or headaches.
May present with flash pulmonary edema, worsening kidney function after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, or unexplained azotemia; symptoms can be masked by other comorbidities.
missing_classic_features: Clear temporal relationship to medication changes

atypical.how_it_differs: Fibromuscular dysplasia is more common in women of childbearing age; severe hypertension may be attributed to preeclampsia, and imaging is limited.
Declining kidney function may be the only clue, especially after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB; blood pressure may be less dramatically elevated.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; blood pressure elevated on repeated readings
general.moderate: Comfortable at rest but with markedly elevated blood pressure; may appear anxious
general.severe: Ill-appearing with severe hypertension; may have signs of heart failure such as dyspnea or edema
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, diaphoretic, in respiratory distress from flash pulmonary edema or with neurologic signs of hypertensive emergency

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff after 5 minutes of rest
findings.finding: Persistent hypertension, often severe and resistant to multiple medications; may differ between arms

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the epigastrium and both upper quadrants with the diaphragm, listening during systole and with the patient supine
findings.finding: Systolic-diastolic bruit over the epigastrium or flank, lateralizing to the side of stenosis
Carotid bruit suggesting concomitant atherosclerotic disease

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the femoral arteries and palpate femoral pulses
findings.finding: Femoral bruit or diminished femoral pulses suggesting peripheral arterial disease

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart at the apex with the bell while the patient lies in the left lateral position
findings.finding: Third heart sound (S3 gallop) indicating volume overload or heart failure

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein at 45 degrees and measure the vertical height above the sternal angle
findings.finding: Jugular venous distension indicating elevated right atrial pressure

findings.maneuver: Press over the dorsum of each foot and the lower tibia for 5 seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Perform a fundoscopic exam after dilating the pupil if needed
findings.finding: Hypertensive retinopathy with arteriolar narrowing, AV nicking, or hemorrhages/exudates

findings.maneuver: Ask about burning with urination and inspect the external genitalia if indicated

labs.caveat: A rise in creatinine of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB is a classic clue to bilateral disease or stenosis in a solitary kidney.
Hypokalemia from secondary hyperaldosteronism; often unmasked or worsened by diuretics.
Proteinuria is usually mild or absent; heavy proteinuria points away from renal artery stenosis and toward primary glomerular disease.
Diabetes and glucose intolerance are common in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis.
Ordered to exclude thyroid disease as a secondary cause of hypertension.
Mild anemia from chronic kidney disease.

findings.finding: Left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria with secondary ST-T changes
ST depression and T-wave inversion in lateral leads from LVH with strain
T-wave inversion in the lateral precordial leads
Evidence of prior myocardial infarction (pathologic Q waves)

imaging.study: Duplex ultrasound of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: First-line screening in most patients; avoids radiation and iodinated contrast

findings.text: Peak systolic velocity in the renal artery above 180–200 cm/s
Turbulent flow with post-stenotic spectral broadening
Parvus-tardus waveform in the intrarenal arteries with a prolonged acceleration time
Reduced kidney size on the affected side
Study limited by body habitus or bowel gas (nondiagnostic)

imaging.study: CT angiography of the abdomen with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Patients with normal kidney function who need detailed anatomy before intervention

findings.text: Focal or ostial narrowing of the proximal renal artery
Atherosclerotic calcification at the ostium or proximal segment

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance angiography of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: Patients who should avoid iodinated contrast or radiation; not used when kidney function is severely reduced because of gadolinium risk

findings.text: Proximal renal artery narrowing with post-stenotic dilatation
String-of-beads appearance in the mid or distal renal artery (fibromuscular dysplasia)

imaging.study: Catheter-based digital subtraction angiography of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: When noninvasive studies are equivocal and revascularization is being considered

findings.text: Direct measurement of the stenosis with a pressure gradient across the lesion

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely used; may be considered when other studies are unavailable and the patient has a single kidney or suspected unilateral disease

findings.text: Reduced uptake and delayed excretion on the affected side after captopril
No specific findings; may show vascular calcification

initial.why: Assesses kidney function, potassium and bicarbonate; a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB is a key clue
Looks for proteinuria, blood or casts that would suggest primary kidney disease instead
Baseline blood count and anemia assessment in chronic kidney disease
Cardiovascular risk assessment in atherosclerotic disease
Screens for diabetes as a cause and accelerator of vascular disease

initial.test: Duplex ultrasound of the renal arteries
initial.why: First-line noninvasive screening test; avoids radiation and contrast

confirmatory.test: CT angiography of the abdomen with IV contrast
confirmatory.why: Defines the anatomy and severity of the stenosis before considering revascularization
confirmatory.only_if: kidney function is adequate and the ultrasound is nondiagnostic or intervention is planned

confirmatory.test: Magnetic resonance angiography of the renal arteries
confirmatory.why: Alternative to CT when iodinated contrast or radiation should be avoided
confirmatory.only_if: CT contrast is contraindicated and kidney function is not severely reduced

confirmatory.test: Catheter-based digital subtraction angiography of the renal arteries
confirmatory.why: Most definitive test; confirms the lesion and measures the pressure gradient when revascularization is planned
confirmatory.only_if: noninvasive studies are equivocal or intervention is being considered

supporting.why: Excludes thyroid disease as another secondary cause of hypertension
Functional assessment of unilateral disease when anatomic imaging is unavailable
supporting.only_if: other imaging is unavailable and unilateral disease is suspected

not_indicated.why: Does not show the renal arteries and does not change management
No role in the evaluation of hypertension or renal artery stenosis
Not routinely needed unless acute coronary syndrome is suspected
Rarely used now that CT, MR and duplex ultrasound are available
not_indicated.only_if: other imaging is unavailable and unilateral disease is suspected

not_indicated.test: CT angiography of the abdomen with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Contrast exposure is not justified when the ultrasound is diagnostic and no intervention is planned
not_indicated.only_if: kidney function is adequate and the ultrasound is nondiagnostic or intervention is planned

not_indicated.test: Magnetic resonance angiography of the renal arteries
not_indicated.why: Gadolinium is avoided in severe kidney impairment
not_indicated.only_if: CT contrast is contraindicated and kidney function is not severely reduced

decision_points: Measure kidney function before contrast imaging; avoid iodinated contrast in advanced kidney disease when possible
Stop or hold nephrotoxic drugs and ensure hydration before angiography
A creatinine rise of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB should prompt evaluation for bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis in a solitary kidney
Revascularization is generally reserved for flash pulmonary edema, refractory hypertension, or deteriorating kidney function rather than for every anatomic stenosis

differential.name: Essential hypertension
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of high blood pressure; most patients with elevated readings have primary hypertension rather than a renovascular cause.

history: Long-standing hypertension that responds to standard medications
No abrupt worsening or loss of control
No flash pulmonary edema or unexplained creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
exam: No signs of widespread atherosclerosis such as carotid or femoral bruits
Blood pressure controlled on one or two agents
labs: No significant creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
imaging: Renal arteries normal on duplex ultrasound or CT angiography if performed

differential.name: Primary aldosteronism
differential.why_considered: A common secondary cause of resistant hypertension that can mimic renal artery stenosis with difficult-to-control blood pressure and hypokalemia.
differential.trigger: Resistant hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic-induced hypokalemia

history: Muscle weakness, cramps, or palpitations from hypokalemia
No history of flash pulmonary edema
exam: Blood pressure elevated but no signs of volume overload
labs: Elevated plasma aldosterone with suppressed renin
imaging: Adrenal nodule or hyperplasia on CT of the adrenals

differential.name: Pheochromocytoma
differential.why_considered: A secondary cause of hypertension that can present with severe, paroxysmal blood pressure elevations and mimic renovascular hypertension.
differential.trigger: Paroxysmal hypertension with headache, palpitations, and sweating

history: Headache, palpitations, and diaphoresis during spells
labs: Elevated plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine metanephrines
imaging: Adrenal mass on CT or MRI

differential.name: Chronic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Kidney impairment is common in renal artery stenosis and can itself cause hypertension and elevated creatinine, making the two difficult to separate.

history: Progressive decline in kidney function over years
exam: Volume overload with edema and crackles
Pallor or uremic signs in advanced disease
labs: No creatinine rise specifically after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
imaging: Renal arteries patent on duplex ultrasound

differential.name: Diabetic nephropathy
differential.why_considered: Diabetes is common in patients with atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis and can cause hypertension with declining kidney function.

history: No abrupt loss of blood pressure control
labs: No creatinine rise specifically after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
imaging: Kidneys normal to enlarged early, small and echogenic late

differential.name: Polycystic kidney disease
differential.why_considered: Can cause hypertension, flank discomfort, and kidney impairment, overlapping with the presentation of renal artery stenosis.

history: Family history of polycystic kidney disease
Hematuria or recurrent urinary tract infections
imaging: Multiple bilateral renal cysts on ultrasound or CT

differential.name: Kidney cancer
differential.why_considered: Renal cell carcinoma can cause hypertension, flank pain, and hematuria, and may be found during workup of resistant hypertension.
differential.trigger: Flank pain with hematuria and a renal mass

history: Weight loss, night sweats, or fever
imaging: Solid enhancing renal mass on CT or MRI

differential.name: Kidney stones
differential.why_considered: Can cause flank pain and hematuria, which may be confused with the flank discomfort sometimes reported in renal artery stenosis.

history: Colicky flank pain radiating to the groin
labs: Normal kidney function or mild elevation

differential.name: Diabetes insipidus
differential.why_considered: Can cause nocturia and polydipsia, which are sometimes reported in renal artery stenosis due to nocturia from hypertension or kidney impairment.

history: Excessive thirst and large volumes of dilute urine

severity.mild: Blood pressure mildly elevated (140–159/90–99 mmHg) on one or two medications; kidney function normal or near normal; no heart failure symptoms
severity.moderate: Blood pressure 160–179/100–109 mmHg despite two or more medications; mild to moderate kidney impairment; may have edema or orthopnea
severity.severe: Blood pressure 180–209/110–119 mmHg despite multiple medications; significant kidney impairment; heart failure symptoms such as crackles or edema
severity.critical: Blood pressure ≥210/120 mmHg with flash pulmonary edema, hypertensive emergency, or rapidly worsening kidney function

red_flags.meaning: Bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis in a solitary kidney; needs urgent evaluation and possible revascularization

red_flags.finding: Creatinine rise of more than 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB
red_flags.meaning: Bilateral disease or stenosis in a solitary kidney; stop the drug and evaluate renal arteries

red_flags.finding: Blood pressure ≥180/120 mmHg with neurologic or cardiac symptoms

red_flags.meaning: Progressive stenosis or atheroembolic disease; may need urgent intervention

red_flags.finding: Abdominal or flank bruit with resistant hypertension
red_flags.meaning: Strongly suggests renovascular disease and should prompt imaging

complications.name: Flash pulmonary edema
clues: Often in bilateral renal artery stenosis

complications.name: Atheroembolic kidney disease
clues: Acute kidney injury after angiography or vascular procedures

complications.name: Left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure

special_populations.differences: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis is most common here; may present with flash pulmonary edema, unexplained azotemia, or worsening kidney function after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB. Symptoms can be masked by other comorbidities.

Fibromuscular dysplasia is more common in women of childbearing age; severe hypertension may be attributed to preeclampsia, and imaging options are limited. ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated.
Declining kidney function may be the only clue, especially after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB; blood pressure may be less dramatically elevated. Contrast imaging requires caution.
Diabetes is common in atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis and can itself cause kidney impairment and hypertension, making the diagnosis harder to separate.
Renal artery stenosis is rare in children; when present it is usually due to fibromuscular dysplasia or a genetic syndrome and presents with severe hypertension, failure to thrive, or headaches.

key_questions.question: How many blood pressure medicines are you on, and are your readings still high?
key_questions.looking_for: Resistant hypertension: blood pressure above goal despite three agents including a diuretic, or control that has been lost after years of good control

key_questions.question: When did your blood pressure first become hard to control?
key_questions.looking_for: Abrupt worsening or new-onset severe hypertension, especially in a younger patient or someone without a family history

key_questions.question: Have you ever had sudden severe shortness of breath, waking up gasping or coughing up pink frothy sputum?
key_questions.looking_for: Flash pulmonary edema, which suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or stenosis in a solitary kidney

key_questions.question: Has your kidney function changed since starting a blood pressure medicine, especially an ACE inhibitor or ARB?
key_questions.looking_for: A creatinine rise of more than about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, a classic clue to bilateral disease or a solitary kidney

key_questions.question: Do you have chest pain with exertion, leg pain when walking, or a history of heart attack, stroke, or aneurysm?
key_questions.looking_for: Atherosclerosis elsewhere (coronary, carotid, peripheral, aortic), which supports atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, high cholesterol, or kidney disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Vascular risk factors and chronic kidney disease that accompany atherosclerotic disease

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or have you smoked?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use, a strong risk factor for atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have high blood pressure, kidney disease, or a blood vessel problem like fibromuscular dysplasia?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of fibromuscular dysplasia or early hypertension, which points toward a non-atherosclerotic cause

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your legs, needing to prop yourself up to breathe, or waking at night short of breath?
key_questions.looking_for: Heart failure from long-standing severe hypertension or volume overload

key_questions.question: Any headaches, dizziness, or vision changes?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of severe or complicated hypertension

key_questions.question: Any burning with urination, blood in the urine, or colicky flank pain radiating to the groin?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, points toward urinary infection, stones, or kidney cancer instead

key_questions.question: Have you had fever, chills, weight loss, or night sweats?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; if present, suggests infection or malignancy rather than renovascular disease

accepted_names: Fibromuscular dysplasia of the renal artery
reasoning_points: Resistant or difficult-to-control hypertension, or loss of previously good control, in an adult with vascular risk factors
Abdominal or flank bruit on auscultation, especially lateralizing to one side
Evidence of atherosclerosis elsewhere (carotid or femoral bruit, prior coronary or peripheral disease)
A creatinine rise of more than about 30% after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB, suggesting bilateral disease or a solitary kidney
Flash pulmonary edema or unexplained heart failure with severe hypertension
Mild or absent proteinuria with otherwise unexplained kidney impairment, arguing against primary glomerular disease
Duplex ultrasound showing elevated peak systolic velocity or a parvus-tardus intrarenal waveform, with confirmatory CT, MR, or catheter angiography
Exclusion of other secondary causes of hypertension such as primary aldosteronism and pheochromocytoma

easy: Older adult with long-standing hypertension that is now uncontrolled on three medications
Known coronary or peripheral arterial disease
Mildly elevated creatinine with a clear rise after starting an ACE inhibitor
medium: Older adult presenting with flash pulmonary edema and severe hypertension
Unexplained azotemia or worsening kidney function without an obvious cause
Younger woman with severe hypertension and a string-of-beads appearance on imaging (fibromuscular dysplasia)
Hypokalemia from secondary hyperaldosteronism that is mistaken for primary aldosteronism
hard: Patient with diabetes and chronic kidney disease where the kidney impairment is attributed entirely to diabetes
Blood pressure only mildly elevated and no bruit, with the clue being a creatinine rise after starting an ACE inhibitor
Nondiagnostic duplex ultrasound due to body habitus or bowel gas, requiring CT or MR angiography
Elderly patient with widespread atherosclerosis and competing causes of kidney impairment, including atheroembolic disease
